- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."

- generate-changelog: Generate a release changelog from conventional commits and upstream baseline notes. Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release. Use before cutting a release branch or when preparing release notes.
- new-component: Scaffold a new Zimmermann component under overrides/app/components/ — TypeScript, Chakra-first, with a paired Storybook story. Use whenever a new custom component is needed.

- pr-checklist: Generate a PR description and merge checklist based on the files changed on the current branch. Pairs with /code-quality.

```
Subject: Follow-up: Enabling the Frontend Team on Claude for Zimmermann

Hi all,

Following up in writing on a point I did not get to make fully in today's meeting.

Our frontend team is three developers, and none of us, myself included, came in with prior hands-on experience on SFCC PWA Kit. I bring an Angular background and prior exposure to AI-assisted development, which let me get up to speed on this stack faster than the rest of the team.

My core position is that Claude can close that experience gap, but only for someone who knows how to use it well. Access to AI does not remove the need for capability, it moves where that capability needs to sit. A skilled driver in a standard car will get further than an inexperienced driver in a supercar. The tool is not the differentiator, the ability to direct it is.

Having closed this gap myself, I believe the team's real challenge is not SFCC PWA Kit itself, but unfamiliarity with the specific, deliberate way we work with Claude on this project, which is more structured than the general AI-assisted coding habits most developers bring in. That mismatch, more than the platform, is the more likely root cause of the hesitation we have seen. I would like to help close it for the rest of the team as well.

My proposal has two parts. First, make the wider team explicitly aware of this context, so the gap and the plan to close it are understood. Second, let me run short, recurring working sessions with the other two developers to walk through approach and strategy, so they build the same working fluency with Claude on this project that I already have.

Separately, on sprint planning, I want to flag a concern with committing to a high volume of user stories in a single sprint at this stage. A significant portion of the stories ahead of us are foundational, with other stories depending on them, so a high volume commitment does not fully reflect that dependency structure. Grouping related stories together for tracking is a separate point I do support, and it does not change this concern.

I also want to acknowledge two dependencies outside our control: the pace of approved, ready-to-build user stories from the business analysts, and designs still in progress with the design team. Both are outside our domain, and the most we can do is keep following up. Where it helps, I would like developers to feel empowered to engage business analysts and designers directly to gather what is needed to scope and build against, rather than waiting on process alone.

Lastly, on design-to-code consistency, Figma-To-React should eventually give us one consistent way of translating designs into code. Until it is ready, I am proposing to take on that role myself in the interim, so the team has one standard to work from in the meantime.

Happy to discuss any of this further.

Kind regards,
Marcel
```

Now let me save the durable context from this (the enablement plan, the sprint stance, and the Figma-To-React tool) to memory for future sessions.

```
Subject: Follow-up: Aligning the Frontend Team on Claude for Zimmermann

Hi all,

Following up in writing on the main point I did not get to land fully in today's meeting: how we, as a frontend team, work with Claude on this project.

We are three frontend developers, and none of us came into this project with prior hands-on experience on SFCC PWA Kit. I am personally known on this team as our Angular developer, which on paper made this React-based stack less natural ground for me than for a React specialist. Even so, prior experience with AI-assisted development let me get up to speed faster than the rest of the team, and that is really the point I want to make.

Having Claude available does not make an experience gap disappear on its own. It only closes that gap for someone who already knows how to direct it well; for someone who does not, the gap is still there, just hidden behind the tool. The comparison I used in the meeting still holds: an experienced driver in a regular car will get further than someone who cannot drive at all, even if you put that second person in a supercar. Claude is the supercar. Knowing how to use it is what actually decides the outcome.

Here is the more specific point. On this project, the harder gap is not SFCC PWA Kit itself; it is that Zimmermann has its own particular, deliberate way of working with Claude, and that is not the general, looser way most developers are used to working with AI. This was not something I was naturally used to either. I had to work through it myself before I could use it effectively here, and closing that gap, more than any platform knowledge, is what let me move as fast as I have. The other two developers have not closed that gap yet, and I believe that, not SFCC PWA Kit itself, is the real source of the hesitation we have seen.

My proposal is to close it deliberately, in two parts. First, make sure the wider team understands this context, so it is clear this is a specific, learnable way of working rather than a personal shortcoming. Second, let me run short, informal working sessions with the other two developers every now and then, where I walk through how I actually think through and approach problems with Claude on this project, so they build the same fluency I already have.

In that same spirit, on design-to-code consistency: Figma-To-React should eventually give the three of us one shared, consistent way of turning designs into code, but it is not ready yet. Until it is, I am proposing to act as that consistency myself, holding our approach to a common standard so we are not each working differently, and so we can move through our committed stories more efficiently in the meantime.

Two smaller items for visibility, since they came up in the same conversation:

- On sprint commitment, I want to flag that many of the user stories ahead of us right now are both foundational and large, with other stories depending on them being finished first. I am not comfortable committing to a high volume per sprint on that basis, though I do support grouping related stories together for tracking, which is a separate question and does not change this.
- Design is still in progress and is critical to development, and the pace of business-analyst-approved, ready-to-build stories is also a factor. Both sit outside our domain to resolve directly; the most we can do is keep following up. Where it helps, I would like developers to feel empowered to reach out to business analysts and designers directly to gather what they need to build against.

Happy to talk through any of this further.

Kind regards,
Marcel
```

Restored: the Angular-developer contrast, "even I wasn't used to this approach either," designs being critical (not just "in progress"), and stories being large as well as foundational.
